# APPENDIX `r new_appendix()`: PARAMETERIZATION OF SARITA CHINOOK OPERATING MODEL {#app:OM}

This appendix describes the parameterziation of the operating model in salmonMSE to incorporate life history variability in hatchery release strategies & natural-origin life cycle groups.
Parameters are organized by life cycle stage.
Sources for the parameters include @ctc2023, @brown2025, as well as the exploitation rate models fitted to various CWT datasets (Appendices \@ref(app:sarita-cwt) and \@ref(app:quinsam-cwt)).

Summary tables of parameters are presented in Tables \@ref(tab:sarita-om-bio) -- \@ref(tab:sarita-om-hatchery).

## Spawners {#sec:spawners}

The egg production is calculated from the number of natural-origin and hatchery-origin spawners. Fecundity is age-specific with fecundity of 3000 at age 3, 3600 at age 4, 4600 at age 5 [@brown2025].

No fish are mature at age 1.

The fecundity at age 2 was set to half of the value of age 3. 
Most if not all age 2 spawners are precocious males. 
Nevertheless, some assumption of fecundity is needed in order to carry over breeding success for age 2 spawners, as they can ensure genetic diversity by breeding across brood years.
Calculations involving spawner composition, including pWILD, PNI, and pHOS are weighted by age class fecundity.

Older age classes more predominantly female, where the proportion female is 0.01 at age 2, 0.1 at age 3, 0.55 at age 4, and 0.8 at age 5 [@brown2025].

A typical value of 0.8 was used for the relative reproductive success of hatchery origin spawners [@withler2018].

## Juvenile natural production

### Egg-fry survival 

Egg-fry survival in the natural environment is modeled as a stochastic density-independent parameter (Figure \@ref(fig:fry-surv)). 
There were egg-fry survival scenarios which varied in the mean value (0.1, 0.15, or 0.2). 
Survival was sampled from a logistic-normal variable:

$$
x_t \sim N\left(\log\left(\dfrac{\mu}{1-\mu}\right), \sigma\right)
$$

where $x$ is a random variable in year $t$, $\mu = 0.1, 0.15, 0.2$, and $\sigma = 1.17$. Survival $s$ is obtained from back-transforming $x$ to normal space (between 0-1): $s_t = \exp(x_t)/(1 + \exp(x_t))$.

The standard deviation which describes inter-annual variability is informed by historical fry/adult data collected in 2017--2023 (Figure \@ref(fig:env)). Fry/adult values were converted to egg-fry survival (mean of approximately 0.09), assuming an average fecundity of 3,900 and a proportion female of 0.4. The survival values were transformed to logistic space to calculate the standard deviation for the sampling function. The historical mean is approximately 0.09.

(ref:fig-fry-surv) Left column: Egg to fry survival sampled stochastically across 3 simulations with three separate means (rows). Right column: Histogram of survival values across 30 projection years and 100 simulation replicates.

### Outmigration

The resulting fry are then divided by life cycle group, which will have different survival rates in age 1, the first year of the marine life stage after outmigration (described in Section \@ref(sec:marine-life-stage)). 
95 percent of the fry as assigned as early-smalls and the rest are late-larges [@brown2025].

## Hatchery production of juveniles

Target hatchery releases, by release strategy, is 500,000 annual releases with a distribution of 335 thousand fed fry and 165 thousand traditionals.
In comparison, the releases in 2023 were 292,853 fed fry and 288,745 traditionals (total of 581,598). 
Release strategies differ in maturity rates, described in Section \@ref(sec:maturity).

The mark rate is assumed to be either one or zero, depending on modeling scenario.

Once brood are collected, the hatchery egg production is calculated assuming 85 percent brood survival. The egg-release survival is 90 percent. Hatchery releases spend little time in the freshwater environment and immediately enter the marine life stage.

### Marine life stage and preterminal fishery {#sec:marine-life-stage}

The juvenile marine life stage is represented in the model through a matrix that indexes semestral age and time (2 semesters equals one year). 

In the first half of the year, juveniles are vulnerable to the preterminal fishery. 
The age-5 exploitation rate is 0.45 (contant through time). This value is the 2013-2018 mean estimated in the Sarita exploitation rate model (ERM, Appendix \@ref(app:sarita-cwt)).

Younger age classes experience lower exploitation rates, determined by the vulnerability at age schedule.
The vulnerability was estimated in the Sarita ERM and was stochastically sampled from the posterior distribution to create the operating model (Appendix \@ref(app:sarita-cwt)).
The vulnerability schedule at age is identical for all release strategies and life cycle groups (Figure \@ref(fig:mat-vul)).

The aggregate calendar year exploitation rate (CYER), using the definition in @ctc2023, is approximately 0.35.

In the second half of the year, mature fish are removed from the juvenile abundance matrix, and the remaining juveniles experience natural mortality. 
For natural-origin juveniles, age-1 natural mortality is 99.6% for early smalls and 95% for late larges. 
For hatchery-origin juveniles, age-1 mortality is 96.9% [Table 3.3 of @brown2025].
For all older fish, the natural mortality is 30% at age 2, 20% at age 3, 10% at age 4 and older, as used in @ctc2023.

### Maturity {#sec:maturity}

CWT escapement indicate that traditionals mature earlier compared to fed fry.
The maturity at age schedule for traditionals was estimated in the Sarita ERM, which used the Robertson (RBT) Creek hatchery as an indicator stock.
However, unlike the Sarita hatchery, the RBT hatchery comprises of only traditionals.
The data series from the Sarita CWT were too short to be used to estimate maturity.
Therefore, the approach was to estimate maturity of fed fry and traditionals from the Quinsam (northern Strait of Georgia) hatchery, using a separate ERM (Appendix \@ref(app:quinsam-cwt)).
The ratio of the differences in maturity from the Quinsam system were then applied to RBT traditional maturity to propose a maturity schedule for the fed fry (Figure \@ref(fig:mat-vul).

In both the Sarita and Quinsam ERM, the maturity schedule is estimated for each brood year. 
For the operating model, the maturity was stochastically sampled from the posterior and averaged across the most recent 6 complete brood years (2013--2018, Figure \@ref(fig:mat-vul)).

It is assumed that both natural-origin life cycle groups (early-smalls and late-larges) have the maturity schedule of fed fry.
The age structure of the return is represented separately from the juveniles. 
The return are only present in the second half of the year and are vulnerable to the terminal marine fishery.

### Terminal fishery 

The age-5 exploitation rate in the marine terminal fishery is 0.24 (constant through time). This value is the 2013-2018 mean estimated in the Sarita ERM (Appendix \@ref(app:sarita-cwt)). 
The relative vulnerability by age class was stochastically sampled from the posterior distribution in the Sarita ERM (Appendix \@ref(app:sarita-cwt)) and assumed to be identical for all release strategies and life cycle groups (Figure \@ref(fig:mat-vul)).

The aggregate CYER is approximately 0.15.

If the fishery is not mark-selective, then hatchery-origin and natural-origin fish experience the same exploitation rate as described above.
If the fishery is mark-selective, then the hatchery-origin exploitation rate is as described above.
The natural-origin fish experience

### In-river return 

After the terminal marine fishery, the in-river return, is represented in a third matrix.
The survival en-route to spawning grounds is one.

The age proportion of strays correspond to values observed in the Sarita CWT for traditionals in 2018, assuming it is representative of strays from adjacent systems (11 percent at age 2, 16% at age 3, 69% at age 4, and 4% at age 5).

### Brood {#app:brood}

Assuming mass-marking (mark rate of 1), the following brood rule is used:

1. Brood is only collected when the in-river return exceeds 600
2. Total brood is the minimum of: (a) 33% of total in-river return and (b) 200% of natural-origin return to river
3. Natural-origin broodtake (NOB) is the smallest among: 50% of natural-origin return to river, (2), and (3)
4. Hatchery-origin broodtake (HOB) is used to reach maximum brood calculated in (2) or until pNOB target is met
5. If necessary, proportionally reduce excess brood (equally between NOB and HOB equally) to prevent exceeding the hatchery release target (calculated from brood fecundity and survival in hatchery).

Two pNOB target values were evaluated: 0.5 and 1.
Brood is non-selective by age class.

Without mass-marking (mark rate of zero), the brood rule is altered as follows:

1. Brood is only collected when the in-river return exceeds 600
2. Total brood cannot exceed 33% of total in-river return 
3. Take brood non-selectively up to the limit in (2), until sufficient brood is obtained to reach release target

### In-river fishery {#app:irf}

After broodtake, in-river harvest occurs with the following rule, assuming mass-marking:

1. Harvest proceeds only if total spawners (the difference between in-river return and broodtake) exceeds 1,300
2. The 1300 spawners includes all natural-origin fish, and any hatchery-origin fish needed to reach the 1,300 threshold
3. Excess hatchery-origin fish are available to in-river fishery

The harvest rate of excess hatchery-origin fish is either zero, 0.25, or 0.75.
Natural-origin fish experience no additional mortality from in-river harvest.

Without mass-marking (mark rate of zero), the catch rule is altered as follows:

1. Harvest proceeds only if total spawners (the difference between in-river return and broodtake) exceeds 1,300
2. All fish exceeding 1300 are available to the fishery which is non-selective

### Fitness

**Text left here, we have fitness calculations but are currently not using them to evaluate the results**

Hatchery-origin spawners can alter the evolutionary fitness of the spawning population in the natural environment. 
The quantitative genetics component of the model calculates fitness of each brood year based on the parental origin [@ford2002].
The parameters for the fitness model are primarily informed by @withler2018.

The population phenotype that is altered by genetic introgression of hatchery spawners is modeled as a Gaussian random variable `z`, with an optimum at 100 in the natural environment and 80 in the hatchery environment. The variance of the phenotype variance ($\sigma^2$) is 10. 

The mean phenotype of a brood year is calculated iteratively from the mean phenotype from parental spawners, accounting for mixed-brood year returns and parental origin, the fitness variance, and the heritability of the phenotype.
Fitness is a cost function calculated from the deviation of the mean phenotype of spawners from the optimum of the natural environment.

The fitness variance ($\omega^2$) is 100, with $\omega^2/\sigma^2 = 10$ implying strong selective pressure. Heritability $h^2$ is stochastic, sampled from a truncated normal distribution with mean of 0.25, standard deviation of 0.15, with bounds of 0 and 0.5.

The equations of Ford (2002) are modified to account for mixed-brood year return, as documented on the [salmonMSE](https://docs.salmonmse.com/articles/equations.html#mixed-brood-year-return) website.

```{r sarita-om-bio, results="as-is"}
sarita_table_bio <- readr::read_csv(here::here("tables/sarita-om.csv")) %>%
  filter(grepl("Bio", Type)) %>%
  select(!Type)

flextable(sarita_table_bio) %>%
  set_caption(
    caption = "Biology, habitat, and harvest parameters organized by life cycle (egg production, freshwater survival, juvenile marine stage, maturity and return). Egg production is calculated from the spawners. Egg-fry survival is density-independent and stochastic. Outmigrants are separated into two groups which differ in migration timing (before/after April) which impacts survival in the first year of the marine life stage."
  ) %>%
  width(j = 1, width = 1.5) %>%
  width(j = 2, width = 3) %>%
  width(j = 3, width = 2)
```

\newpage

```{r sarita-om-hatchery, results="as-is"}
sarita_table_hatch <- readr::read_csv(here::here("tables/sarita-om.csv")) %>%
  filter(Type == "Hatchery") %>%
  select(!Type)

flextable(sarita_table_hatch) %>%
  set_caption(
    caption = "Hatchery parameters. The simulated broodtake is back-calculated from target releases, brood survival in hatchery, and fecundity. The brood composition is determined by the target pNOB, subject to a maximum brood-escapement ratio for natural origin fish. Hatchery releases are divided into two groups, fed fry and traditionals, which differ in the timing and size at release. While the survival is identical between release strategeies, traditionals mature earlier than fed fry."
  ) %>%
  width(j = 1, width = 1.5) %>%
  width(j = 2, width = 3) %>%
  width(j = 3, width = 2)
```
